justice: The massive width of the vehicular roadway compared to the narrow pedestrian spaces reflects a lack of equity in spatial resource distribution for non-motorized users.
The absence of tactile paving on the sidewalks significantly reduces fairness for visually impaired pedestrians navigating the street.
Traffic signal poles placed directly in the middle of the right-side sidewalk create physical barriers, hindering accessibility for wheelchair users and mobility scooters.
safety: The long zebra crossing spanning multiple lanes without a pedestrian refuge island increases exposure time and crossing risk for slower-moving elderly and disabled users.
The complete lack of separated bike lanes forces cyclists of all ages, including vulnerable teenagers and older adults, to share the roadway with motor vehicles.
A motor vehicle turning directly over the pedestrian crosswalk highlights potential intersection conflicts, threatening the safety of all crossing pedestrians.
livability: The absence of street furniture, such as benches or resting spots along the stone balustrade, reduces livability for elderly pedestrians who need to rest.
The lack of active ground-floor commercial units or community spaces fails to attract teenagers or families, resulting in a desolate and car-centric atmosphere.
The presence of a long, impermeable fence and balustrade restricts social interaction and surveillance (eyes on the street) from adjacent properties.
sustainability: The expansive impervious asphalt surface without visible swales or permeable paving limits ecological stormwater management.
The lack of dedicated cycling infrastructure fails to support low-carbon, active travel options for all user groups.
Street trees are planted but have small canopies, providing minimal green infrastructure support and limited carbon offset potential.
aesthetics: The uniform white, multi-story buildings on the right side provide a cohesive and tidy architectural backdrop.
The visible mountain range in the background enhances the natural scenic quality and visual appeal of the streetscape.
Overhead power lines on the left side and somewhat cluttered utility poles detract from the overall visual neatness of the environment.
comfort: The sparse, bare trees offer no shade cover, which would result in poor thermal comfort for vulnerable pedestrians like the elderly during hot weather.
The complete lack of seating facilities along the walking paths negatively impacts the physical comfort of older adults and disabled individuals requiring rest.
The proximity of the unprotected sidewalk to wide, multi-lane traffic reduces the psychological comfort of pedestrians due to noise and perceived exposure.
walkability: The exceptionally wide zebra crossing makes traversing the road physically demanding and time-consuming for elderly and mobility-impaired users.
Obstacles like utility poles blocking the narrow sidewalk path disrupt walking continuity for pedestrians and wheelchair users.
The lack of visually engaging street frontages or shade makes the walking experience monotonous and unattractive for all social groups.
bikeability: The absence of marked or protected bike lanes forces cyclists into mixed traffic on a wide road, severely reducing safety and bikeability for teenagers and seniors.
The wide intersection and crosswalk area lack clear routing, bike boxes, or painted guidance to help cyclists navigate safely around turning vehicles.
There are no visible bicycle parking facilities near the buildings, reducing the convenience and feasibility of cycling for active commuters.
